blocks.content: An **array** is a contiguous block of memory that stores elements of the same type. Elements are accessed by their index in **O(1)** time.
Key operations and their time complexities:
A **dynamic array** automatically resizes when it runs out of capacity. When full, it allocates a new array (typically *2x* the size) and copies elements over.

The **amortized** cost of append is *O(1)* because resizing happens infrequently.
A **linked list** stores elements in nodes, where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike arrays, elements are not stored contiguously in memory.

**Sorting** is one of the most fundamental operations in computer science. Sorted data enables efficient searching (binary search), simplifies data analysis, and is a prerequisite for many algorithms.
Common sorting algorithms and their complexities:
**Merge sort** is a *divide-and-conquer* algorithm. It splits the array in half, recursively sorts each half, then merges the sorted halves.
Merge sort guarantees ***O(n log n)*** time in all cases but requires *O(n)* extra space for the merge step.
**Quick sort** picks a pivot element, partitions the array around it (elements smaller than the pivot go left, larger go right), and recursively sorts each partition.
Quick sort is ***O(n log n)*** on average and sorts **in-place** (no extra array needed), making it very cache-friendly and fast in practice.
A **tree** is a hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges. Key terminology:

**Root** — The topmost node
**Parent** — A node with children
**Leaf** — A node with no children
**Height** — Longest path from root to a leaf
**Depth** — Distance from the root to a node
A **binary tree** is a tree where each node has at most *two* children: a left child and a right child.
A **binary search tree (BST)** maintains the invariant that for every node, all values in the left subtree are *smaller* and all values in the right subtree are *larger*.
In a balanced BST, search, insert, and delete are all ***O(log n)***. In the worst case (a skewed tree), they degrade to *O(n)*.
There are three standard depth-first traversals of a binary tree:

**In-order** — Left, Root, Right (gives sorted order for BSTs)
**Pre-order** — Root, Left, Right
**Post-order** — Left, Right, Root
An **in-order** traversal of a BST visits nodes in ascending sorted order.
